related_questions.question: Does diabetes affect your gums?
related_questions.snippet: Did you know diabetes can also cause problems in your mouth? People with diabetes have a higher chance of having periodontal (gum) disease, an infection of the gum and bone that hold the teeth in place. Periodontal disease can lead to pain, persistent bad breath, chewing difficulties, and even tooth loss.

related_questions.question: How to heal diabetic gums?
related_questions.snippet: Taking care of your teeth and gums correctly, such as with regular brushing and flossing, can help prevent mouth problems linked to diabetes. When you have diabetes, you can also keep your teeth and gums healthy by controlling your blood sugar level and getting regular dental check-ups.

text_blocks.snippet: Stage 2 gum disease, also known as early periodontitis, is a more advanced stage of gum disease than gingivitis. It involves inflammation and potential bone loss around the teeth. Symptoms can include bad breath, receding gums, and gums that bleed easily when brushing or flossing. Treatment typically involves scaling and root planing, a deep cleaning procedure to remove plaque and tartar from under the gums.

list.snippet: Progression from Gingivitis: If gingivitis (inflammation of the gums) is not treated, it can progress to early periodontitis, or Stage 2.
Inflammation and Bone Loss: At this stage, inflammation has spread to the bone that supports the teeth, and some bone loss may be visible on dental X-rays.
Gum Recession: The gums may start to pull away from the teeth, forming pockets.
Persistent bad breath.
Gum recession (gums appear to be pulling away from the teeth).
Gums that bleed easily when brushing or flossing.
Mild bone loss around the teeth.
Increased sensitivity to hot or cold.

list.title: Scaling and Root Planing:
list.snippet: This deep cleaning procedure removes plaque and tartar from both above and below the gum line, as well as smoothing the tooth root surfaces to prevent further bacterial buildup.

list.title: Home Care:
list.snippet: Consistent brushing and flossing, along with regular dental checkups, are crucial for managing the disease.

list.title: Early intervention is key:
list.snippet: Treating gum disease in its early stages can prevent further progression and more serious complications.

list.title: Professional care is needed:
list.snippet: While good oral hygiene is important, it's not enough to treat early periodontitis. Professional scaling and root planing are necessary.

list.title: Ongoing maintenance:
list.snippet: Even after treatment, regular dental visits are essential to monitor the condition and prevent recurrence.

text_blocks.snippet: Diabetes and gum health are closely linked. Poorly controlled diabetes can increase the risk and severity of gum disease (periodontal disease), and gum disease can, in turn, make it harder to manage blood sugar levels. Managing both diabetes and oral health is crucial for overall well-being.
snippet_highlighted_words: Diabetes and gum health are closely linked

list.title: Increased Risk of Gum Disease:
list.snippet: High blood sugar levels can lead to increased bacteria in the mouth, promoting plaque formation and inflammation.

list.title: More Severe Gum Disease:
list.snippet: Individuals with diabetes may experience more aggressive forms of gum disease and slower healing times.

list.title: Increased Risk of Tooth Loss:
list.snippet: Diabetes is a significant factor in tooth loss, with 1 in 5 cases linked to the disease.
Difficulty Controlling Blood Sugar: Gum disease can make it harder to manage blood glucose levels.
Increased Risk of Complications: Severe gum disease is associated with an increased risk of diabetes-related complications like heart and kidney problems.

list.title: Good Oral Hygiene:
list.snippet: Brush teeth at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and a soft brush, and floss daily.

list.title: Regular Dental Checkups:
list.snippet: See a dentist regularly (every six months or more frequently if advised).

list.title: Control Blood Sugar:
list.snippet: Maintaining good blood sugar control is essential for both preventing and managing gum disease.

list.title: Consider Water Flossers:
list.snippet: Water flossers, especially those with a specialized tip like the Pik Pocket™ tip by Waterpik, can be beneficial for reducing gingivitis symptoms in people with diabetes.

list.title: Manage Dry Mouth:
list.snippet: If experiencing dry mouth, use sugar-free gum or candies, drink plenty of water, and consider using a humidifier at night.

list.title: Seek Prompt Treatment:
list.snippet: If you experience any signs of gum disease (red, swollen, or bleeding gums, receding gums, loose teeth, bad breath), see your dentist promptly.

list.title: Consider Diabetes Screening:
list.snippet: A dentist may recommend screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes based on the severity of gum disease.
